guide.howItWorks: A small chainsaw bar on the end of a 2–4 m pole, battery-powered, used from the ground to limb conifers up to about 2 m and to take out branches overhanging the roof. The fire job it does is breaking the ladder fuel — the continuous line of branches that lets a ground fire climb into the crowns and then into your roofline.
guide.market: Battery pole saws are now a mature consumer category with three tiers. Entry-level 20 V units at CAD $150–$300 handle branches up to about 100 mm and run 20–30 minutes. Mid-range 40–60 V platform tools at CAD $300–$650 are the sweet spot for a homeowner clearing an acre. Professional 80 V and petrol units at CAD $700–$1,500 are for people doing this for days at a time. The single most important buying factor is not the saw — it is whether it shares a battery platform with tools you already own, because batteries are most of the cost.

features.label: Reach
features.detail: Fixed or telescoping, typically 2.4–4 m of total reach with your arms. More reach means more weight at the end of a lever, which is what tires you.

features.label: Bar length
features.detail: 200–250 mm is standard and is enough for FireSmart limbing. Longer bars are heavier and rarely needed overhead.

features.label: Battery platform
features.detail: Buy into a platform you already have or intend to build on. A second battery roughly doubles your working session and costs CAD $100–$250.

features.label: Auto-oiling
features.detail: Worth having. Manual oiling on a pole saw is forgotten, and a dry chain wrecks the bar.

features.label: Weight and balance
features.detail: The specification nobody checks and everybody feels after twenty minutes. Under 5 kg extended is the difference between finishing the job and finishing half of it.

costs.upfront: CAD $200–$650 for a capable homeowner unit with one battery.
costs.consumables: Bar oil, CAD $15–$25 a year. Chains, CAD $20–$40 each — expect one or two a season if you hit dirt.
costs.ancillary: A second battery, CAD $100–$250. Helmet with face shield, CAD $60–$120 — not optional overhead. Chaps if you also own a ground chainsaw.
costs.fiveYear: CAD $150–$400 in chains, oil and eventually a battery, which lose capacity after 3–5 years.

differentiators.label: Versus a petrol pole saw
differentiators.detail: Battery wins for homeowner use: no mixing, no starting drama after eight months in the shed, quieter, lighter. Petrol wins only if you are cutting all day.

differentiators.label: Versus hiring an arborist
differentiators.detail: A day of professional limbing and thinning is CAD $600–$2,000 and gets far more done, safely, with the debris hauled away. If you have more than about twenty trees, hiring is often the better value — and it is definitively better for anything requiring a ladder or a climb.

differentiators.label: Versus a hand pruning saw on a pole
differentiators.detail: CAD $50, no batteries, entirely adequate for branches under 50 mm, and considerably safer overhead. Genuinely worth owning alongside.

differentiators.label: What limbing actually achieves
differentiators.detail: Removing branches to 2 m breaks the path from ground fire to crown. It is one of the highest-value tasks in FireSmart's Zone 1 guidance and it costs only your Saturday.

buying.where: Any hardware or big-box store, outdoor power equipment dealers, Amazon.
buying.note: Pick the platform first, the saw second. If you already own 40 V batteries, buy the bare tool and save CAD $150.

install.time: Assembly 15 minutes; the actual work is 1–3 days spread over a spring
install.note: Working overhead with a saw is the most dangerous thing on this entire site. Never cut above shoulder height on a ladder, never cut what you cannot step back from, and stop when you are tired — which will be sooner than you expect. Anything near a power line is a utility's job, not yours.

ongoing.note: Limbing is not a one-time task — conifers regrow and new ladder fuel appears every few years. Plan a spring walk-around annually and a real session every two to three years. Chain sharpening or replacement as you go.

alternatives.name: A manual pole pruning saw
alternatives.note: CAD $40–$90, safer, slower, fine for smaller branches. Buy one regardless.

alternatives.name: An arborist for a day
alternatives.note: CAD $600–$2,000, far more progress, debris removed, no ladder risk to you.

guide.verdict: A good buy if you have trees and a Saturday habit. If you have a lot of trees, or any of the work needs a ladder, the money is better spent on a professional day than a better saw.

name: McLeod Fire Rake / Hoe
priceNote: One-time buy
summary: The combination rake-and-hoe wildland crews use to scrape fuel down to mineral soil. Ideal for clearing needle litter, cutting a small control line and smothering spot fires.
pros: Two tools in one
Nearly indestructible
Cheap
cons: Heavy for extended use
bestFor: Needle-litter cleanup and spot-fire response.

guide.howItWorks: A wildland hand tool: a heavy rake head with coarse tines on one side and a flat hoe blade on the other, on a long handle. You pull litter and duff away with the tines and scrape down to mineral soil with the blade. It is the tool for building the bare-ground breaks in Zone 0 and for clearing needle litter from under decks, along fences and around outbuildings.
guide.market: A century-old US Forest Service pattern, now made by a dozen manufacturers from CAD $60 imports to CAD $200 forged professional heads. The difference is real: a stamped-steel head on a cheap handle will bend on the first serious root, while a forged head on hickory will outlive you. Council Tool and a handful of similar makers own the quality end. There is no wildfire-branded premium version worth buying — this is a fire-service commodity and should be priced like one.

features.label: Dual head
features.detail: Tines for raking litter, flat blade for scraping to mineral soil and for cutting light roots. Two tools in one is the point.

features.label: Forged versus stamped head
features.detail: The quality question. Forged survives leverage against roots and rock; stamped bends.

features.label: Hickory or fibreglass handle
features.detail: Both fine. Hickory is repairable and traditional; fibreglass survives being left in the rain.

features.label: Length
features.detail: Standard handles are around 1.2–1.5 m, which gives the leverage the work needs.

costs.consumables: None. A file for the blade edge, CAD $15.
costs.ancillary: Gloves. A tarp for hauling duff.
costs.fiveYear: Nil. A forged McLeod is a lifetime tool.

differentiators.label: Versus a leaf rake and a garden hoe
differentiators.detail: You probably own both, and together they do most of this. The McLeod is faster, tougher and does not break on a root — but if the choice is between buying one and doing the work with what is in the shed, do the work.

differentiators.label: Versus a leaf blower
differentiators.detail: A blower moves loose needles off a driveway and out of gutters far faster. It does not scrape duff to mineral soil, which is the part that matters in Zone 0. Own both.

differentiators.label: What it is for
differentiators.detail: The specific FireSmart task: getting the first 1.5 m around the house down to gravel, pavers or bare mineral soil, with no bark mulch, no needle litter and nothing that carries flame to the wall.

differentiators.label: The honest framing
differentiators.detail: This is the cheapest item in a category where the real cost is your labour. The tool is a rounding error; the eight hours of raking is the purchase.

buying.where: Forestry supply houses, farm and ranch supply, Amazon, and some hardware stores in fire-prone regions.
buying.note: Buy forged if you have rocky or rooty ground. Buy anything if you do not — it is a rake.

install.time: None. It is a hand tool.
install.note: Nothing to assemble beyond fitting the head on some models.

ongoing.note: The tool needs nothing. The work is annual: needle litter and duff rebuild every season, and Zone 0 has to be re-cleared each spring. Put it in the calendar.

alternatives.name: A stiff leaf rake plus a garden hoe
alternatives.note: Already in your shed. Slower, breaks sooner, does the job.

alternatives.name: A leaf blower
alternatives.note: Much faster for loose litter on hard surfaces, useless for duff.

guide.verdict: Buy it if you like good tools; skip it without guilt if you own a rake and a hoe. Either way the clearing is what protects the house, and no tool does that part for you.

name: 72-Hour Emergency Kit (2–4 person)
priceNote: Customize after purchase
summary: A pre-built backpack with water, food, first aid, light and warmth for 72 hours. Treat it as a starting point: add medications, documents, chargers, cash and respirators.
pros: Everything in one grab
Water and food already packed
cons: Generic contents — always customize
Check expiry dates annually
bestFor: Every household in an evacuation-prone area.

guide.howItWorks: A pre-assembled bag holding water, food, light, first aid, a radio, and basic sanitation for two to four people for three days — the standard planning horizon Public Safety Canada and FEMA both use, because that is roughly how long it takes for organised assistance to reach a displaced population. In a wildfire evacuation the realistic use is different from an earthquake: you are more likely to be in a hotel or a reception centre than in a field, so the kit's real job is that you left with something rather than nothing.
guide.market: Pre-built emergency kits are a crowded consumer market with wide quality variance and consistent overpricing. Cheap kits at CAD $60–$120 contain a lot of items of no value — tiny torches, a whistle, twelve adhesive bandages — chosen because they raise the item count on the box. Serious kits at CAD $200–$500 have real water, real food with a real shelf life, and a first aid kit somebody thought about. Above that you are usually buying a nicer bag. Building your own from good components costs roughly the same as a mid-range kit and is meaningfully better, at the price of a Saturday.

features.label: Water and purification
features.detail: The heaviest and most important element. 4 L per person per day is the standard, which is heavy — most kits compromise with pouches plus a filter or tablets.

features.label: Food with real shelf life
features.detail: Look for 5-year-rated ration bars or freeze-dried meals with dates on them, not granola bars that expire in eight months.

features.label: Light and power
features.detail: A hand-crank or battery lantern plus headlamps. Headlamps beat torches because they leave your hands free.

features.label: First aid
features.detail: The component most often padded out. Check for trauma dressings and a tourniquet rather than a hundred small bandages.

features.label: Radio
features.detail: Crank or battery, ideally with the weather band. Overlaps with a dedicated weather radio, and the dedicated one is better.

features.label: Sanitation and warmth
features.detail: Emergency blankets, wipes, bags. Unglamorous, disproportionately valuable.

costs.upfront: CAD $150–$500 for a credible 2–4 person kit.
costs.consumables: Water, food and batteries rotate on a 3–5 year cycle. Budget CAD $60–$150 per refresh.
costs.ancillary: The wildfire-specific additions almost no kit includes: N95 or P100 respirators for everyone, copies of documents, prescription medication, pet food and a carrier, phone chargers and a battery bank, cash in small bills.
costs.fiveYear: CAD $250–$700 including one full consumables refresh.

differentiators.label: Versus building your own
differentiators.detail: Building your own is better and costs about the same. The pre-built kit's advantage is that it exists — the DIY kit that is still a list on your phone protects nobody. Buy the kit, then upgrade the weak components.

differentiators.label: What wildfire kits specifically need
differentiators.detail: Respirators, because smoke lasts weeks after the fire. Document copies. Medication. Pet supplies. Chargers. Most generic kits contain none of these and it is the gap that matters.

differentiators.label: The car versus house question
differentiators.detail: In a wildfire the kit's value is in the vehicle. A perfect kit in a basement you did not have time to re-enter is worth nothing. Keep it by the door you leave from, or in the car through fire season.

differentiators.label: Price sanity
differentiators.detail: Above about CAD $500 you are buying luggage. Spend the difference on a second set of respirators and a battery bank.

buying.where: Canadian Red Cross and provincial emergency-preparedness shops, outdoor retailers, Amazon, Costco seasonally.
buying.note: Read the actual contents list, not the item count. Check the food and water expiry dates before you accept the delivery.

install.time: An hour to unpack, check and personalise
install.note: Open it when it arrives. Add the personal items — medication, documents, respirators, chargers, pet supplies — and make sure everyone in the house knows where it lives and can carry it.

ongoing.note: Diarise a spring check every year: expiry dates, battery corrosion, medication rotation, and whether the clothing still fits the children. This is the item most likely to be technically present and functionally useless.

alternatives.name: Building your own from a checklist
alternatives.note: Better contents, same money, needs a Saturday you have to actually spend.

alternatives.name: A grab-list on the fridge plus your existing camping gear
alternatives.note: Free, works if you are organised, fails under stress. A list is not a bag.

guide.verdict: Buy one, then fix it — add respirators, documents, medication and chargers, and keep it by the door. The most common failure in this category is not a bad kit, it is a good kit in the wrong room.

name: Fireproof & Waterproof Document Bag
priceNote: Silica-fibre pouch
summary: A silica-fibre pouch for passports, insurance policies, deeds, and a USB drive of scanned records. Lives in the go-bag, not the filing cabinet.
pros: Inexpensive
Holds a laptop-size stack of documents
cons: Fire-rated for minutes, not hours — it's for the go-bag, not for leaving behind
bestFor: Everyone.

guide.howItWorks: A silicone-coated fibreglass pouch that resists flame and radiant heat for a stated period, usually with a water-resistant closure. It protects passports, deeds, insurance policies, birth certificates and a backup drive either in a safe at home or as a grab item. Understand what it is: heat and flame resistance for a limited time, not a safe.
guide.market: A crowded, low-cost Amazon category full of near-identical products with impressive-sounding temperature claims and very little third-party verification. Prices run CAD $25–$90. Almost every listing claims something like '2000 °F for 30 minutes', typically from an in-house test at whatever conditions favoured the number. Above this tier sit genuinely rated fire safes, which are UL-classified, cost CAD $200–$900 and weigh 25–90 kg. There is very little in between, and the gap is where most buyers' expectations sit.

features.label: Silicone-coated fibreglass
features.detail: The standard construction. Effectively all credible bags use it; the differences are layer count and stitching.

features.label: Closure type
features.detail: Velcro plus a zip is better than either alone. The closure is usually the weak point in any real fire exposure.

features.label: Size
features.detail: Get one that fits legal-size documents flat. Folding a deed into a small pouch is how people end up not using it.

features.label: Water resistance
features.detail: Matters more than people expect — anything that survives a fire in a house has usually also been hosed.

costs.consumables: None.
costs.ancillary: A USB drive or two for scanned copies, CAD $15–$40.
costs.fiveYear: Nil.

differentiators.label: Versus a rated fire safe
differentiators.detail: A UL-classified safe is verified, heavy and stays put. A bag is unverified, light, and leaves with you — which for wildfire is arguably the more useful property, since evacuation is the likely scenario.

differentiators.label: Versus cloud backup
differentiators.detail: Scanning everything to encrypted cloud storage costs nothing, survives total loss of the building, and is what actually protects you. The bag protects originals; the scan protects the information. Do the scan first — it is free and takes an evening.

differentiators.label: The claims problem
differentiators.detail: Treat the temperature and duration figures as marketing unless there is a named test standard behind them. Very few in this category have one.

differentiators.label: Where you put it
differentiators.detail: A grab bag by the door is more useful than a bag in a basement safe. The wildfire failure mode is not that the bag failed, it is that nobody picked it up.

buying.where: Amazon in both countries, office supply, hardware stores.
buying.note: Buy the size up. Nearly everyone regrets the small one.

install.time: An evening, mostly scanning
tools: A phone scanner app or a flatbed scanner
install.note: Scan everything to encrypted cloud storage first, then put the originals in the bag, then put the bag where you will actually grab it. The scanning is the real work and the real protection.

ongoing.note: Review contents annually — passports expire, insurance policies change, and the list of what matters shifts. Update the scans at the same time.

alternatives.name: Encrypted cloud backup of scanned documents
alternatives.note: Free, better, survives total loss. Do this whether or not you buy the bag.

alternatives.name: A UL-classified fire safe
alternatives.note: CAD $200–$900, actually verified, stays in the house. Good for what you cannot replace and will not carry.

alternatives.name: A safe deposit box
alternatives.note: The old answer. Still a good one for originals you rarely need.

guide.verdict: Cheap, mildly useful, and no substitute for scanning everything to the cloud tonight. Buy it if you want the originals to travel with you; do the scan regardless.

name: N95 / P100 Respirators (family pack)
priceNote: Buy several sizes to find fit
summary: NIOSH-approved N95 or P100 masks for every person in the house, including during evacuation drives through smoke. Fit is everything; a valved P100 half-mask is far more comfortable for extended wear.
pros: Cheap
The single most effective smoke-health product
cons: Poor fit = little protection
Not made for children under ~7
bestFor: Everyone in a smoke-affected region.

guide.howItWorks: A certified particulate respirator filters the fine particulate — PM2.5 — that makes up most of the health burden of wildfire smoke. N95 filters at least 95% of airborne particles; P100 filters at least 99.97% and is oil-resistant. Both work only if the seal against your face is good, which is why fit matters more than filter rating and why beards defeat them entirely.
guide.market: Post-2020, respirators are a large, well-supplied and unfortunately heavily counterfeited market. The split that matters: disposable N95 filtering facepieces at CAD $2–$6 each, and reusable half-face elastomeric respirators with P100 cartridges at CAD $40–$120 plus CAD $20–$50 per cartridge pair. For a household facing weeks of smoke every summer, elastomerics are cheaper over three years and seal better. Certification is the buying signal: NIOSH approval in the US, and in Canada look for NIOSH or the CSA Z94.4-compliant equivalents. A 'KN95' from an unverifiable seller is a gamble.

features.label: NIOSH certification
features.detail: The approval number should be printed on the mask itself. Check it against the NIOSH certified equipment list — it takes two minutes and rules out most counterfeits.

features.label: N95 versus P100
features.detail: For smoke, N95 is adequate. P100 filters more and, in an elastomeric, seals better and lasts far longer.

features.label: Fit and sizing
features.detail: The whole ballgame. A poorly sealed P100 protects less than a well-fitted N95. Buy sizes for the actual faces in your house, including children's — most adult masks do not seal on a child.

features.label: Exhalation valve
features.detail: More comfortable for long wear. Fine for smoke; irrelevant to anything else you might have been told.

features.label: Not for gases
features.detail: Particulate filters do nothing for carbon monoxide or VOCs. Nothing in this category makes a smoke-filled structure safe to be in.

costs.upfront: CAD $30–$80 for a family pack of disposables; CAD $60–$150 per person for an elastomeric with cartridges.
costs.consumables: Disposables last roughly a day of heavy smoke exposure each. P100 cartridges last weeks to months of intermittent use.
costs.ancillary: Nothing.
costs.fiveYear: CAD $150–$500 for a household that has several smoke weeks a year. Elastomerics come out well ahead over that period.

differentiators.label: Versus a surgical or cloth mask
differentiators.detail: Neither seals and neither filters PM2.5 meaningfully. They are not smoke protection and it is worth being blunt about that, because a great many people spent 2023 wearing one outdoors believing otherwise.

differentiators.label: Versus staying indoors with a purifier
differentiators.detail: Clean indoor air is the primary strategy and the better one. Respirators are for the times you have to be outside — moving the car, checking the property, walking the dog.

differentiators.label: The beard problem
differentiators.detail: Facial hair at the seal line defeats a respirator completely. This is not a soft recommendation. If you will not shave, a powered air-purifying respirator with a hood is the only real option and it is CAD $500 and up.

differentiators.label: Children
differentiators.detail: There is no NIOSH-certified respirator for small children. Smaller adult sizes fit some older children. For young children, indoor air quality is the only real control.

buying.where: Industrial safety suppliers — the best source by a distance — hardware stores, pharmacies, Amazon.
buying.note: Buy from a safety distributor rather than a marketplace if you can. Counterfeits are common on marketplaces and impossible to spot from a photograph. Verify the NIOSH number on arrival.

install.time: 10 minutes to fit-check each person
install.note: Do a user seal check on every person: cover the filter, inhale, and feel the mask pull in with no leak at the edges. If it leaks at the nose bridge or cheeks, the size is wrong. Doing this once in the spring means nobody is learning it at midnight in an orange sky.

ongoing.note: Replace disposables when they get hard to breathe through, damp or soiled. Store elastomerics in a sealed bag — cartridges absorb from the air even unused. Check the household stock every spring.

alternatives.name: Elastomeric half-face respirator with P100 cartridges
alternatives.note: Better seal, better economics over a few seasons, less comfortable in heat.

alternatives.name: Staying indoors with filtered air
alternatives.note: The primary strategy. Respirators supplement it.

guide.verdict: The cheapest health protection on this site and the one most people already own the wrong version of. Buy certified, check the seal on each person in the spring, and understand that clean indoor air — not the mask — is the main defence.

name: HEPA Air Purifier (large room)
priceNote: Size by CADR to your bedroom
summary: A true-HEPA purifier with a high smoke CADR rating, sized to give 4–5 air changes an hour in your bedroom. Run continuously through smoke events and keep spare filters on hand.
pros: Measurably reduces PM2.5 indoors
Helps year-round with allergens
cons: Filters are a recurring cost
One unit per room, not per house
bestFor: Bedrooms and the room where kids or elders spend the day.

guide.howItWorks: A fan pulls room air through a true HEPA filter, which captures at least 99.97% of 0.3 µm particles — comfortably including wildfire smoke PM2.5. Run continuously in a closed room, it drives indoor particulate well below outdoor levels. The relevant metric is CADR, the clean-air delivery rate, which combined with room size tells you how many air changes per hour you actually get.
guide.market: A large, mature and confusing consumer market. The useful structure: budget units at CAD $150–$300 with real HEPA and modest CADR; mid-range at CAD $300–$700 covering a genuine bedroom or living room; premium at CAD $700–$1,500 mostly buying quieter operation, app control and design. The distortions to watch are subscription filter models, which can double lifetime cost, and units sold on room-size claims that assume one air change an hour — nowhere near enough for smoke. AHAM Verifide CADR ratings are the one independent number in the category and are worth insisting on.

features.label: True HEPA filter
features.detail: Not 'HEPA-type', 'HEPA-like' or '99% at 2 microns'. True HEPA is a defined standard; the alternatives are marketing.

features.label: CADR, verified
features.detail: The number to compare. For smoke, aim for 4–5 air changes per hour: CADR in cfm should be roughly your room's floor area in sq ft times ceiling height, divided by about 12.

features.label: Activated carbon stage
features.detail: Handles some of the smell and VOCs in smoke that HEPA does not touch. Thin carbon-dusted pre-filters do very little — look for actual carbon weight.

features.label: Noise at working speed
features.detail: The specification that decides whether it runs all night. A unit quiet on low and useless on low is a common trap — check dB at the speed you would actually need.

features.label: Filter cost and availability
features.detail: Check the replacement filter price and whether it is proprietary before you buy the machine.

features.label: No ozone
features.detail: Avoid ionisers, plasma and UV add-ons. Some generate ozone, which is a respiratory irritant. A fan and a filter is the whole technology you need.

costs.upfront: CAD $250–$700 for a unit that genuinely covers a bedroom or living room during smoke.
costs.consumables: Filters, CAD $60–$180 each, every 6–12 months — and much faster in a heavy smoke season. Budget two sets in a bad year.
costs.ancillary: One unit per bedroom is the realistic target, so multiply. A MERV-13 furnace filter for the whole house, CAD $30–$70.
costs.fiveYear: CAD $600–$1,600 per unit including filters. Filters are most of the lifetime cost, which is why the subscription models deserve scrutiny.

differentiators.label: Versus a Corsi-Rosenthal box
differentiators.detail: A CR box costs a quarter as much and often delivers more CADR, because it is a big fan and a lot of filter area. It is louder, larger and looks like what it is — a box fan taped to furnace filters. For a bedroom during a smoke week, it is objectively good value.

differentiators.label: Versus a MERV-13 furnace filter
differentiators.detail: The furnace filter treats the whole house whenever the fan runs and costs CAD $40. Do that first. Then add purifiers in bedrooms, which is where the hours are.

differentiators.label: The sizing mistake
differentiators.detail: Manufacturer room-size claims usually assume a single air change per hour. For smoke you want four or five. In practice: buy for a room roughly a quarter of the size on the box.

differentiators.label: Where to put it
differentiators.detail: Bedrooms, doors closed, running continuously through the smoke event. Eight hours of clean air while asleep beats a purifier in an open-plan living room nobody sits in.

buying.lead: Same day, except during a major smoke event when the entire country buys them at once
buying.where: Big-box, Costco, Amazon, appliance retailers.
buying.note: Buy in winter. In August 2023 purifiers were sold out across western Canada within days, and the ones still available were the ones nobody wanted.

install.time: 5 minutes
install.note: Unpack, remove the plastic wrap from the filter — a genuinely common oversight — place it away from walls and curtains, and run it.

ongoing.note: Filter changes are the commitment. In a heavy smoke season a filter can be exhausted in weeks, not months. Keep a spare, and check the pre-filter monthly — vacuuming it doubles the main filter's life.

alternatives.name: Corsi-Rosenthal box
alternatives.note: A quarter the price, more airflow, much louder. Genuinely competitive on performance.

alternatives.name: MERV-13 furnace filter with the fan on continuous
alternatives.note: CAD $40, treats the whole house, should be your first move.

guide.verdict: Buy one per bedroom, size by CADR rather than the claim on the box, and buy them in February. Do the MERV-13 furnace filter first — it is a tenth the price and covers the whole house.

name: Corsi-Rosenthal Box (DIY: box fan + 4 MERV-13 filters)
priceNote: Box fan + four 20×20 MERV-13 filters + tape
summary: A box fan taped to a cube of four MERV-13 furnace filters. Peer-reviewed testing shows it rivals commercial purifiers costing several times more. Build one per room.
pros: Very cheap for the airflow
Parts available at any hardware store
cons: Loud on high
Not pretty
bestFor: Whole-house coverage on a budget.

guide.howItWorks: A 20 inch box fan taped to a cube of four MERV-13 furnace filters, blowing outward. The large filter area means low resistance, so a cheap fan moves a great deal of air through a great deal of media. It was designed in 2020 by Richard Corsi and Jim Rosenthal as an open, unpatented answer to expensive purifiers, and independent testing has repeatedly found it competitive with commercial units several times its price.
guide.market: There is no market, which is the point — it is a public-domain design assembled from commodity parts. What exists commercially is kits at CAD $80–$180 that bundle the filters and a shroud, and a few boutique versions in tidy cases at CAD $250–$400. Buying the parts separately is cheapest: a box fan is CAD $35–$70 and MERV-13 filters are CAD $15–$30 each. Filter quality is the only real variable; buy from a known furnace-filter brand rather than the cheapest listing.

features.label: Very high CADR for the money
features.detail: Typically 600–900 cfm, which exceeds most CAD $500 consumer purifiers. Four filters' worth of surface area is why.

features.label: MERV-13 media
features.detail: Captures PM2.5 effectively. Not HEPA-grade per pass, but it processes so much more air per hour that total particle removal is comparable or better.

features.label: Cardboard shroud
features.detail: A simple cardboard ring around the fan outlet improves airflow measurably — by roughly 20–50% in published testing. Do not skip it.

features.label: Cheap consumables
features.detail: Replacement filters are ordinary furnace filters at CAD $15–$30, available everywhere, with no proprietary lock-in.

features.label: Repairable and scalable
features.detail: Build a second one for another bedroom in twenty minutes.

costs.upfront: CAD $100–$180 for fan, four filters and tape. A pre-packaged kit runs CAD $120–$200.
costs.consumables: Four filters per change, CAD $60–$120. Change every 6–12 months, or every few weeks in dense smoke.
costs.ancillary: Duct tape or foil tape, and a piece of cardboard.
costs.fiveYear: CAD $400–$700 including filter changes — well under half the cost of a comparable commercial purifier.

differentiators.label: Versus a commercial HEPA purifier
differentiators.detail: More airflow per dollar and much cheaper filters. Louder, physically large, and it looks like a taped box fan in your bedroom. That aesthetic objection is the honest reason most people buy the commercial unit instead, and it is a legitimate reason.

differentiators.label: Noise
differentiators.detail: A box fan on high is 55–65 dB. Many people cannot sleep next to it. Running on medium sacrifices some CADR and is usually the practical compromise.

differentiators.label: Safety
differentiators.detail: Use a fan with a fused plug and a thermal cut-out — fans made after roughly 2012 generally have both. Do not leave any box fan running unattended for days in a room with children, and do not obstruct the intake.

differentiators.label: The community angle
differentiators.detail: Schools, community centres and band offices across BC and Alberta have built these by the dozen during smoke seasons. If you want to help a neighbourhood breathe, this is the cheapest way to do it at scale.

buying.lead: Same day — fans sell out in heat waves, filters rarely do
buying.where: Hardware and big-box stores for both components. Kits from a few online sellers.
buying.note: Buy the fan in spring. Box fans vanish from shelves in the first heat wave, which is usually the same week the smoke arrives.

install.time: 20–30 minutes to build
install.note: Filters go with the airflow arrows pointing in toward the fan. Fan blows outward, out the top. Tape the seams properly — leaks bypass the filters entirely. Add the cardboard shroud; it is free performance.

ongoing.note: Filters darken visibly, which is a useful indicator no commercial unit gives you. Change all four when they are grey. In a heavy season that may be twice.

alternatives.name: A commercial HEPA purifier
alternatives.note: Quieter, tidier, more expensive to buy and to feed.

alternatives.name: A single filter taped to a fan
alternatives.note: Works, but a quarter of the filter area and a much noisier, less effective result. Build the cube.

guide.verdict: The best performance per dollar in clean air, and the reason to buy a commercial purifier instead is noise and appearance, not effectiveness. Build one for the room where people sleep.

name: Indoor/Outdoor PM2.5 Monitor
priceNote: Indoor units are cheaper than outdoor sensors
summary: A laser particle counter that tells you actual PM2.5 in your bedroom, so you can decide when purifiers are winning and when it's safe to ventilate. Outdoor units also contribute to public smoke maps.
pros: Real data instead of guessing
Outdoor units help your neighbours too
cons: Consumer sensors read high in humidity
bestFor: Anyone running purifiers seriously.

guide.howItWorks: A laser particle counter draws air past a beam and counts the scattering events, converting them to an estimated PM2.5 concentration in µg/m³. It tells you what the air in a specific room actually is, rather than what a regional monitoring station 40 km away reports. That distinction matters, because indoor concentrations during a smoke event can be anywhere from a tenth to well above the outdoor reading depending on your building.
guide.market: Consumer air monitors split cleanly. Cheap handheld units at CAD $40–$120 use uncalibrated sensors and drift badly — useful for relative changes, not for absolute numbers. Mid-range fixed monitors at CAD $150–$400 (PurpleAir, AirGradient, Awair and similar) use Plantower or Sensirion sensor modules with reasonable calibration and log data over time. Reference-grade instruments start around CAD $3,000 and are not a consumer product. The mid-range is where the value is, and PurpleAir in particular feeds a public map that has become genuinely useful infrastructure during western North American smoke seasons.

features.label: Laser scattering sensor
features.detail: Plantower and Sensirion modules dominate and are decent. The brand on the box often matters less than which module is inside — worth asking.

features.label: Indoor and outdoor variants
features.detail: An outdoor unit tells you when to close up; an indoor unit tells you whether it worked. If you buy one, buy the indoor one.

features.label: Data logging and history
features.detail: The real value. A number now is mildly interesting; a graph across a week tells you whether your purifier and your window discipline are working.

features.label: Public network contribution
features.detail: PurpleAir outdoor units publish to a public map, which improves local awareness in exactly the rural areas government monitors do not cover.

features.label: Humidity correction
features.detail: Laser sensors over-read in high humidity. The better units and networks apply a correction; the cheap handhelds do not.

costs.upfront: CAD $150–$400 for a credible unit.
costs.consumables: None, though the sensor module degrades over roughly 3–5 years of continuous use.
costs.ancillary: Power and Wi-Fi. Outdoor units need weather-protected mounting.
costs.fiveYear: Purchase price plus eventual replacement. Some units allow a CAD $40 sensor module swap, which is worth checking.

differentiators.label: Versus government AQHI or AirNow
differentiators.detail: Free, reference-grade, and possibly measuring a valley you do not live in. During smoke events the difference between the station reading and your street can be large. A local monitor resolves that.

differentiators.label: Versus the PurpleAir public map
differentiators.detail: If a neighbour already runs an outdoor unit, you get their outdoor data free. What you still lack is your indoor number, which is the actionable one.

differentiators.label: What it changes
differentiators.detail: This is a behaviour device. It tells you when to close windows, when it is safe to open them again, whether the purifier in the bedroom is winning, and whether the filter needs changing. Without it people guess, and they mostly guess wrong in the direction of opening windows too early.

differentiators.label: Accuracy expectations
differentiators.detail: Expect ±10–20% against reference in the ranges that matter. That is plenty for deciding whether to open a window and not enough for any clinical purpose.

buying.lead: Days to a few weeks; PurpleAir units have historically backordered during major smoke events
buying.where: Direct from the manufacturers, Amazon, some electronics retailers.
buying.note: Decide indoor or outdoor before you buy — they are different products and the indoor one is the more useful single purchase.

install.time: 15 minutes including Wi-Fi setup
install.note: Put it at breathing height, away from the kitchen, the fireplace and any purifier's outlet — all three will give you nonsense readings. Cooking will spike it; that is the sensor working, not a fault.

ongoing.note: Keep the intake dust-free. Note that readings drift upward over years as the sensor ages; a wildly high baseline on a clear day means it is time for a new module.

alternatives.name: The free AQHI or AirNow apps
alternatives.note: Free, well-calibrated, potentially measuring somewhere else. Use them as well.

alternatives.name: A neighbour's PurpleAir on the public map
alternatives.note: Free outdoor data. Does not tell you about your own indoor air.

guide.verdict: The cheapest way to find out whether everything else you bought for smoke is actually working. Buy the indoor one first.

name: Emergency Weather Radio (NOAA / Weatheradio Canada)
priceNote: Get one with SAME alerting and battery backup
summary: A dedicated weather radio with SAME county/region alerting wakes you up for evacuation orders even when cell networks are congested. Weatheradio Canada broadcasts on the same frequencies.
pros: Independent of internet and cell
Alarm wakes you at night
cons: Alert coverage varies by region — check your local transmitter
bestFor: Rural homes and anywhere cell coverage is weak.

guide.howItWorks: A dedicated receiver tuned to the seven VHF weather-band frequencies used by NOAA Weather Radio in the US and Weatheradio Canada north of the border. Both networks broadcast continuously from a national transmitter grid and carry emergency alerts, including evacuation orders relayed through the national alerting systems. A SAME-equipped radio sits silent until an alert coded for your specific county or forecast region is transmitted, then sounds an alarm loud enough to wake a household. It runs entirely on broadcast RF: no internet, no cell tower, no app, no subscription.
guide.market: This is a small, stable and largely commoditised category dominated in North America by Midland, with Sangean, Eton and Kaito making up most of the rest. Prices run CAD $35–$150. The market divides into three real tiers rather than the many the packaging implies. Bottom tier, CAD $25–$50: crank or battery radios with a weather band but no SAME alerting — they receive the broadcast if you turn them on, which is not the same as being warned. Middle tier, CAD $50–$110: desktop SAME alert radios with AC power, battery backup and county programming. This is the tier that does the job. Top tier, CAD $110–$200: adds better antennas, external alert outputs for accessibility devices, and rugged or marine builds. Nothing above the middle tier meaningfully improves the chance you are woken up, and the price differences within the middle tier are mostly about display and ergonomics rather than radio performance.

features.label: SAME alerting
features.detail: Specific Area Message Encoding. You program the code for your county or forecast region and the radio ignores everything else. Without it you either listen to a live broadcast permanently or you rely on a general alert tone for a region far larger than yours — which people mute after the third false relevance.

features.label: Battery backup
features.detail: The radio must survive a power cut, because power goes down in the same events that generate the alerts. Look for AC power with AA or a sealed backup, not battery-only.

features.label: Alert volume and tone
features.detail: The functional specification is whether it wakes you through a closed bedroom door. Desktop units are considerably louder than handhelds.

features.label: External antenna jack
features.detail: The difference between reception and no reception in a valley. If you are rural, insist on it — a CAD $25 external wire antenna can turn an unusable signal into a solid one.

features.label: Alert-type filtering
features.detail: Better units let you select which event codes trigger the alarm, so you are not woken for a marine advisory. Useful, but do not filter so aggressively that you miss something.

features.label: Accessibility outputs
features.detail: Some models drive bed-shakers and strobes. Relevant, and the reason the top tier exists.

costs.upfront: CAD $45–$110 / USD $35–$85 for a SAME desktop unit — the tier worth buying.
costs.consumables: Backup batteries. Three AA every 12–18 months, roughly CAD $10 a year. Alkaline leakage is the main way these radios die, so check them annually.
costs.ancillary: An external antenna, CAD $20–$60, if you are in a valley or a basement. Nothing else — there is no subscription, no account and no app.
costs.fiveYear: Roughly CAD $100 all in, including the radio. It is the cheapest warning system available to a household by a wide margin.

differentiators.label: Versus phone alerts
differentiators.detail: Alert Ready in Canada and WEA in the US push emergency alerts to phones and they work well. They also depend on a cell network that congests badly during major incidents, on a phone that is charged, and on a phone that is not on silent in another room. The radio's entire value is that it fails differently. Own both.

differentiators.label: Versus a wildfire app
differentiators.detail: Apps give richer information: perimeters, wind, evacuation-zone maps. They need data connectivity to give it. The radio gives you one thing, loudly, with no network.

differentiators.label: SAME versus no SAME
differentiators.detail: The single differentiator in this category. A CAD $35 crank radio without SAME is a radio you would have to already be listening to. Do not buy that one for this purpose.

differentiators.label: Canadian coverage caveat
differentiators.detail: Weatheradio Canada's transmitter network is dense in populated corridors and thin in parts of the North and interior. Check the Environment and Climate Change Canada transmitter map for your postal code before you buy. If there is no transmitter within range, this product will not work for you, and no amount of antenna solves it.

differentiators.label: What it will not do
differentiators.detail: It relays official alerts. It does not detect fire, it does not know where the fire is, and it will not tell you anything your provincial agency has not broadcast. It is a doorbell, not an oracle.

buying.where: Canadian Tire, Home Hardware and most Canadian big-box retailers; Walmart, Home Depot, Lowe's and electronics retailers in the US; Amazon in both countries; and marine and outdoor suppliers, which often carry better-built models than the general retailers.
buying.note: The easiest purchase on this site — but check the transmitter map first, because in a handful of Canadian regions the honest answer is that reception is not there. Verify the model says SAME on the box, not merely 'weather alert'.

install.time: 20–40 minutes, nearly all of it programming
tools: Nothing — a pen to write down your SAME code
install.note: The install is trivial; the programming is where people give up. Look up your SAME code on the NOAA or ECCC site before you start — it is a six-digit number for your county or forecast region, and if you live near a boundary you should program the neighbouring one as well. Then run the radio's self-test, and put it in the bedroom, not the basement. A correctly programmed radio in the wrong room has failed.

ongoing.note: Press the test button monthly — most units also receive a weekly test broadcast, so you will know within days if reception has been lost. Replace backup batteries annually and check for leakage. Re-check your SAME code if you move.

alternatives.name: Alert Ready / WEA phone alerts
alternatives.note: Free, already on your phone, network-dependent. Use them as well, not instead.

alternatives.name: A provincial wildfire app plus a smart speaker routine
alternatives.note: Richer information, entirely internet-dependent.

alternatives.name: A neighbourhood phone tree
alternatives.note: Unfashionable, and in rural communities with poor coverage it is still the thing that actually works.

guide.verdict: Under CAD $100 for a warning system that does not care whether the cell network is up. Check your transmitter coverage first, buy a SAME model, spend the twenty minutes programming it, and put it in the bedroom. It is the first thing we would buy and the one most people skip.

name: Outdoor Wi-Fi Camera (solar or battery)
pick: Check on your home after evacuating
priceNote: Pair with a battery backup on your router
summary: A camera pointed at the house and the approach lets you see smoke, spot fires and whether the sprinklers are running — from the evacuation centre. Solar units keep working through short outages.
pros: Remote situational awareness
Also useful as ordinary security
cons: Dead if the internet goes down — add router backup power
bestFor: Anyone who evacuates early (which should be everyone).

guide.howItWorks: A battery or solar-powered Wi-Fi camera pointed at the approach to your property, giving you a live view from wherever you are. In a wildfire context it does one specific thing well: it lets you see smoke, ember fall or fire behaviour at your house after you have evacuated, which is the difference between knowing and refreshing a news site for three days.
guide.market: An enormous, fast-moving consumer market — Ring, Reolink, Arlo, Eufy, Wyze and dozens more — at CAD $80–$400 per camera. The fire-relevant considerations are unusual and narrow the field sharply: it has to run without mains power, it has to reach the internet without your house Wi-Fi if the power goes, and it has to survive heat and smoke. Most of the market fails at least two of those. The ones that pass are solar-powered LTE cameras, which are a small and more expensive subset at CAD $300–$600 plus a data plan.

features.label: Solar or long battery life
features.detail: Mains power fails early in these events. A solar panel and a decent battery keeps the camera up when the house does not.

features.label: LTE option
features.detail: The critical one, and the one most buyers miss. A Wi-Fi camera dies with your router. An LTE camera keeps reporting as long as the cell tower stands.

features.label: Local plus cloud recording
features.detail: Cloud footage survives the building. Local-only storage burns with the camera.

features.label: Weather and temperature rating
features.detail: Check the operating range. Many consumer cameras top out around 45–50 °C, which a wall in radiant heat will exceed long before flames arrive.

features.label: Subscription terms
features.detail: Many brands paywall cloud storage and even basic notifications. Read what you are committing to before the hardware discount tempts you.

costs.upfront: CAD $150–$600 per camera; the solar LTE units that actually suit this use are at the top of that.
costs.consumables: None.
costs.ancillary: LTE data plan, CAD $10–$30 a month. Cloud storage subscription, CAD $5–$20 a month. These recur and are most of the five-year cost.
costs.fiveYear: CAD $900–$2,500 per camera once subscriptions are counted. Price the plan, not the camera.

differentiators.label: Versus a neighbour with a phone
differentiators.detail: Cheaper, more reliable and more informative, if you have one who stays. Most people do not, which is why the camera exists.

differentiators.label: Versus provincial fire perimeter maps
differentiators.detail: Free and authoritative at the landscape scale. They will not tell you whether your shed is standing. Different questions.

differentiators.label: The honest limitation
differentiators.detail: This is an information product, not a protection product. It changes nothing about whether the house survives. What it changes is your ability to make decisions — whether to send someone back, what to tell your insurer, and whether to stop refreshing a map at 3 a.m.

differentiators.label: Wi-Fi dependence is the usual failure
differentiators.detail: A camera on house Wi-Fi and house power goes dark in the first hour of a major event, exactly when it becomes useful. If you buy one for this reason, buy the LTE version or accept that it is a general-purpose security camera.

buying.where: Big-box electronics, Amazon, security specialists for the LTE models.
buying.note: Check LTE coverage at the property before committing to a cellular model, and check the subscription price over three years, not the sticker.

install.time: 30–60 minutes per camera
install.note: Mount high, angle to cover the approach and the most exposed elevation, and point the solar panel south. Test the view remotely on cell data with your home Wi-Fi turned off — that is the scenario it is for.

ongoing.note: Clean the lens and solar panel each spring, verify remote access before fire season, and re-check that the subscription is still active. A lapsed plan is a dead camera you think is alive.

alternatives.name: A neighbour who stays and a phone
alternatives.note: Free and better, when available.

alternatives.name: Provincial wildfire perimeter maps and satellite hotspot feeds
alternatives.note: Free, authoritative, landscape scale.

guide.verdict: Buy it for peace of mind after you leave, not for protection — and only in the solar LTE configuration, because the ordinary Wi-Fi version goes dark exactly when you would want it.

name: Portable Power Station (500–1,000 Wh)
priceNote: Look for a unit with pass-through UPS mode
summary: Keeps the router, cameras, phones and a purifier running through the power shutoffs that increasingly accompany high fire danger. Also the heart of a vehicle evacuation kit.
pros: Silent, indoor-safe
Solar-rechargeable
cons: Won't run a fire pump — that needs gas
bestFor: Everyone in an area with public safety power shutoffs.

guide.howItWorks: A lithium battery, an inverter and a set of outlets in a case. It runs the things that matter when the grid drops: the Wi-Fi router, phone charging, a CPAP machine, a HEPA purifier, some lights and a laptop. It does not run your house, and understanding that boundary is most of buying one well.
guide.market: A crowded and rapidly maturing market — EcoFlow, Jackery, Bluetti, Anker and many others — where capacity per dollar has improved sharply. The useful tiers: 300–600 Wh at CAD $350–$700 for phones, lights and a router; 1,000–2,000 Wh at CAD $900–$2,200, which will also run a purifier, a CPAP for several nights or a fridge intermittently; and 2,000 Wh and up at CAD $2,000–$5,000, approaching generator territory. The chemistry split matters: LiFePO4 cells cost more and last 3,000–6,000 cycles, while older NMC packs last 500–800. For a device you cycle rarely and want to still work in ten years, LiFePO4 is the right answer.

features.label: Capacity in watt-hours
features.detail: The honest number. Divide by the wattage of what you want to run for a rough runtime: a 50 W purifier on a 1,000 Wh station is about 18 hours after losses.

features.label: Continuous output wattage
features.detail: Separate from capacity and just as important. A 1,000 Wh station with a 600 W inverter will not start a fridge compressor regardless of how full it is.

features.label: LiFePO4 chemistry
features.detail: Longer life, better heat tolerance, less degradation from sitting at full charge. Worth the premium for an emergency device.

features.label: Solar input
features.detail: Turns it from a battery into a supply. A 200 W panel recharges a 1,000 Wh unit in roughly a clear day — much less in heavy smoke, which is worth knowing before you rely on it.

features.label: Pass-through charging
features.detail: Lets it work as a UPS for the router, which is the single most useful everyday function.

features.label: Pure sine wave output
features.detail: Required for medical devices such as CPAP. Check explicitly.

costs.upfront: CAD $900–$2,200 for the 1,000–2,000 Wh band most households want.
costs.consumables: None. The battery itself degrades — LiFePO4 to roughly 80% capacity after several thousand cycles, which for emergency use is effectively never.
costs.ancillary: Solar panels, CAD $300–$900 for a useful 200–400 W. A car charging cable.
costs.fiveYear: Purchase price. Expect to replace the unit at 8–12 years, not 5.

differentiators.label: Versus a petrol generator
differentiators.detail: A CAD $900 generator produces far more power for far less money and refuels in a minute. It is also loud, cannot run indoors, needs stored fuel, needs starting, and is a fire risk in its own right during a fire event. The power station is silent, indoor-safe and starts by pressing a button. For running a router and a purifier, the station wins; for running a well pump or a whole fridge for a week, the generator does.

differentiators.label: Versus a fire pump's needs
differentiators.detail: It will not run a fire pump. Petrol pumps are petrol for a reason. Do not conflate the two purchases.

differentiators.label: The realistic wildfire use
differentiators.detail: Communications and clean air. Router, phones, a purifier in one bedroom, lights, and any medical device. That is a genuinely valuable list and it fits comfortably in 1,000–2,000 Wh.

differentiators.label: Solar in smoke
differentiators.detail: Dense smoke can cut solar output by half or more. Plan your recharge assumptions accordingly — this is the detail that catches people out in exactly the scenario they bought it for.

buying.lead: Days; frequently discounted, so waiting for a sale is rational
buying.where: Amazon, Costco, big-box, direct from manufacturers.
buying.note: Buy on watt-hours and continuous watts, and insist on LiFePO4. Ignore the marketing capacity names, which are not standardised.

install.time: Minutes
install.note: Charge it fully on arrival. Work out now which outlet the router is on, and label the cable — in a power cut at night people plug in the wrong things.

ongoing.note: Recharge every 3–6 months even unused; a battery left flat for a year may not recover. Store between 20–80% charge if the manufacturer supports it, in a cool place. Test the whole setup annually.

alternatives.name: A petrol generator
alternatives.note: More power, less money, more noise, outdoors only, needs fuel stored on a property you are trying to keep from burning.

alternatives.name: A large USB power bank
alternatives.note: CAD $60–$150. Runs phones for days. Does not run a purifier or a CPAP, and for many people phones is the whole requirement.

guide.verdict: Sized right — 1,000–2,000 Wh, LiFePO4 — it covers communications, clean air and medical devices through a multi-day outage. It is not a generator substitute and it will not run anything to do with water.

name: 5-Gallon Backpack Fire Pump (Indian / Smith-style)
priceNote: Trombone-style hand pump; no batteries or gas
summary: The refillable water backpack every wildland crew carries. Knocks down spot fires on mulch, decks and grass with a directed stream. Fill it from any bucket or tank.
pros: Refillable, no consumables
Precise aim
Works with no power
cons: Heavy when full (~20 kg)
bestFor: Spot fires after the front passes.

guide.howItWorks: A 5 gallon (about 19 L) water tank worn on the back, with a hand-operated trombone pump that throws a stream 8–12 m or a fine spray for wetting down. It is the wildland crew's tool for mopping up spot fires and knocking down small ignitions, and it is genuinely the right tool for the specific homeowner job of chasing embers that have landed in the yard, on the deck or in the gutter.
guide.market: A small, stable market of essentially two designs: the traditional galvanised or stainless Indian-pattern tank at CAD $180–$400, and lighter poly-bag versions at CAD $120–$250. Smith, Indian and a handful of forestry suppliers dominate. Build quality tracks price honestly here, and stainless units last decades. There is little to confuse you — the main decision is metal versus poly, which is a weight-versus-durability trade.

features.label: 19 L capacity
features.detail: Roughly 19 kg on your back when full. That is the real constraint — it is a substantial load and it dictates how far from the tap you can usefully work.

features.label: Trombone pump
features.detail: Two-handed, continuous, no priming and nothing to fail. Adjustable from a straight stream for reach to a fog for cooling.

features.label: Metal versus poly tank
features.detail: Stainless lasts a lifetime and takes rough handling; poly is 2–3 kg lighter and cheaper. Galvanised sits in between and eventually rusts.

features.label: Refill opening
features.detail: A wide mouth matters more than it sounds — you will refill from a bucket, a tank or a creek, not a tidy tap.

features.label: Straps and frame
features.detail: The difference between usable and miserable. Padded shoulder straps and a waist belt on anything you might carry for an hour.

costs.consumables: Pump seals every few years, CAD $20–$40 for a kit.
costs.ancillary: Nothing required. A wetting agent or Class A foam concentrate, CAD $40–$120, roughly triples effectiveness on duff and is worth having.
costs.fiveYear: Under CAD $100 in seals. A stainless unit is a lifetime purchase.

differentiators.label: Versus a garden hose
differentiators.detail: The hose has unlimited water and a fixed radius. The backpack goes anywhere — the far fence, the back of the shed, the neighbour's roof edge — and keeps working when the tap has no pressure. Both, not either.

differentiators.label: Versus a fire extinguisher
differentiators.detail: An extinguisher gives you 10–20 seconds of discharge for a fire that is already established. A backpack pump gives you fifteen minutes of water for embers and spot fires. Different problems, and the pump matches the wildfire problem better.

differentiators.label: The physical reality
differentiators.detail: 19 kg on your back, in heat and smoke, pumping with both hands. This is real work and it is worth being honest about who in the household can actually do it.

differentiators.label: The right job for it
differentiators.detail: Post-frontal patrol. Once the main front has passed, embers keep landing and small ignitions keep starting for hours. That is when houses that survived the front are still lost, and that is exactly what this tool is for.

buying.where: Forestry and firefighting supply houses, farm and ranch supply, wildfire equipment specialists, Amazon.
buying.note: Buy stainless if you can stretch to it. Check the strap arrangement — the cheap ones are punishing after ten minutes.

install.time: Minutes
install.note: Fill it and carry it around the property once, so you know what 19 kg feels like and where you would refill. Practise the pump action — it is not obvious the first time.

ongoing.note: Empty and dry after use — water left in a galvanised tank rusts it out. Store dry, keep it full and accessible through fire season if you can lift it that way, and replace pump seals when the stroke goes soft.

alternatives.name: A garden hose with a good nozzle
alternatives.note: Unlimited water, limited reach, dies with the pressure.

alternatives.name: A wheeled 100 L tank sprayer
alternatives.note: More water, no back strain, useless on rough ground or stairs.

alternatives.name: Buckets
alternatives.note: Not a joke. Slower, free, and how a great many houses have been saved.

guide.verdict: The right tool for the hours after the front passes, which is when a lot of surviving houses are lost. Buy stainless, and be honest with yourself about who can carry 19 kg.

name: 10 lb ABC Fire Extinguisher (garage & deck)
priceNote: Rechargeable metal-valve models last decades
summary: A 10 lb ABC extinguisher gives you 20+ seconds of discharge, versus 8 seconds from a kitchen model. Mount one at the garage door and one by the deck. Choose rechargeable metal-valve units.
pros: Much more capacity than kitchen units
Handles wood, electrical and fuel fires
cons: Dry chemical is messy — that's fine, it's a fire
bestFor: Every garage and deck.

guide.howItWorks: A pressurised cylinder of monoammonium phosphate dry chemical rated for Class A (ordinary combustibles), B (flammable liquids) and C (energised electrical). It gives you roughly 20–25 seconds of discharge at 6–8 m. In a wildfire context it is not for fighting fire — it is for the small ignition on the deck, in the garage or in the vehicle that becomes a house fire if nobody catches it in the first minute.
guide.market: A commodity market with real certification behind it, which is unusual and welcome. Amerex, Kidde, First Alert and Buckeye cover most of the retail supply at CAD $50–$150 for a 10 lb ABC unit. The meaningful distinctions are the UL rating stamped on the label, whether the valve is metal or plastic, and whether the unit is rechargeable. Rechargeable metal-valve extinguishers cost roughly double and can be serviced for decades; disposable plastic-valve units are thrown away after any use or after roughly twelve years. For a house, buy rechargeable.

features.label: UL rating
features.detail: Look for something like 4-A:60-B:C on the label. The numbers are tested performance, not marketing. A 10 lb unit typically rates 4-A:60-B:C; a 5 lb, about 3-A:40-B:C.

features.label: 10 lb size
features.detail: The right size for a garage or a deck. The common 2.5 lb kitchen unit gives about 9 seconds of discharge, which is not much when you are nervous.

features.label: Metal valve and rechargeable
features.detail: Serviceable, refillable, lasts decades. Plastic-valve disposables are landfill after one squeeze.

features.label: Pressure gauge
features.detail: Check it monthly. Dry chemical can settle and units lose pressure slowly; the gauge is the only warning you get.

features.label: Mounting bracket
features.detail: Included on most. Use it — an extinguisher on the floor behind boxes is not an extinguisher.

costs.upfront: CAD $60–$150 each for a rechargeable 10 lb ABC. Two or three around a property is sensible.
costs.consumables: None until used.
costs.ancillary: Mounting brackets if not supplied. A second and third unit — garage, deck, vehicle.
costs.fiveYear: CAD $30–$60 per unit for a recharge or a professional inspection if you use one or your insurer wants documentation. Otherwise nil.

differentiators.label: Versus a backpack pump
differentiators.detail: The extinguisher is 20 seconds and instant; the pump is fifteen minutes and needs carrying. For a flaring barbecue or a smouldering deck board, the extinguisher. For patrolling a yard after ember fall, the pump.

differentiators.label: Versus a garden hose
differentiators.detail: The hose is better for almost every Class A wildfire-adjacent situation — it does not run out in 20 seconds. The extinguisher's advantage is that it handles fuel and electrical fires the hose makes worse, and it is instantly to hand.

differentiators.label: Where they should be
differentiators.detail: Garage, kitchen, deck or barbecue area, and each vehicle. The garage matters most — it is where fuel, batteries, solvents and a woodpile usually share a room.

differentiators.label: The realistic limit
differentiators.detail: A 10 lb extinguisher addresses a fire the size of a wastebasket or a small deck ignition. Against anything larger it does nothing except delay your departure. If it does not go out in the first ten seconds, leave.

buying.where: Hardware stores, big-box, Costco, fire-protection suppliers, Amazon.
buying.note: Check the UL rating on the label and buy rechargeable with a metal valve. The CAD $30 saving on a disposable is not a saving.

install.time: 10 minutes
install.note: Mount it at the exit side of the room, so you are never reaching past a fire to get it. Show everyone in the household where it is and run through PASS — pull, aim at the base, squeeze, sweep — out loud once. That five-minute conversation is most of the value.

ongoing.note: Check the gauge monthly. Invert and shake annually to loosen settled powder. Service or replace at the manufacturer's stated interval — typically 6 years for a service, 12 for hydrostatic testing or replacement.

alternatives.name: A fire blanket for the kitchen
alternatives.note: CAD $25, better for a pan fire, no mess, no substitute for an ABC unit elsewhere.

alternatives.name: A garden hose on a reel by the deck
alternatives.note: More water, better for Class A, wrong for fuel and electrical.

guide.verdict: Cheap, certified and genuinely useful for the small ignition that would otherwise become the house fire. Buy rechargeable 10 lb units, mount them by the exits, and be clear with yourself that ten seconds of no progress means you leave.

name: Hardwired Interconnected Smoke Alarm
priceNote: Per unit; a whole house is 4-8 of them
summary: Mains-powered with battery backup, wired so that any one alarm sets off every alarm in the house. This is what building codes require in new construction in both countries, and the configuration that performs best in real fires.
pros: Operated in 93% of fires in NFPA's data, against 79% for battery-only units
Any alarm sounds all of them — a basement fire wakes a third-floor sleeper
Battery backup covers power cuts, which often accompany fires
cons: Needs an electrician unless the wiring already exists
Retrofitting into a finished house is disruptive and usually not worth opening walls for
bestFor: New construction, gut renovations, and any house that already has alarm wiring in place.

guide.howItWorks: A 120 V circuit powers the alarm and keeps a backup battery charged. A third conductor — the interconnect wire — carries a signal between units, so when one detects smoke it triggers every alarm on the loop. Newer systems achieve the same thing over a radio link instead of a wire.
guide.market: This is a two-brand market in North America. Kidde and First Alert (BRK) between them hold most of the shelf space, with a long tail of Universal, Ecoey and house brands. Prices run CAD $25 to $70 per unit. The real differentiators are sensor type, whether the unit is combination smoke/CO, and whether interconnection is wired or wireless — not brand. Every unit sold legitimately in Canada or the US is tested to UL 217 or CAN/ULC-S531, so the certification is a floor rather than a selling point.

features.label: Interconnect wiring
features.detail: The third wire is the whole point. Codes in both countries require that when more than one alarm is needed, any one sounds all of them within the dwelling.

features.label: Battery backup
features.detail: Required by code and the reason the hardwired failure rate is low. Power failure accounted for only 7% of alarm failures in NFPA's data.

features.label: Sensor type
features.detail: Ionisation is faster on flaming fires, photoelectric on smouldering ones. Dual-sensor units exist and are what USFA recommends if you are not mixing types across the house.

features.label: UL 217 8th edition or later
features.detail: The current standard adds smouldering and flaming polyurethane tests plus a cooking nuisance test. Worth checking, because when NIST tested 45 models against the new criteria, not one met all of them.

features.label: Wireless interconnect option
features.detail: Listed wireless interconnection is accepted for retrofits in the US and in Ontario for houses with secondary suites. Elsewhere in Canada the code language still says wired — check before relying on it.

costs.upfront: CAD $25-$70 per alarm. A typical two-storey house with basement needs five to eight.
costs.consumables: Backup batteries every year or two on units that have replaceable ones.
costs.ancillary: Electrician time if the wiring is not there — commonly CAD $150-$400 per location, which is what makes retrofit uneconomic.
costs.fiveYear: Essentially the purchase price. The whole unit is replaced at ten years from manufacture regardless of condition.

differentiators.label: Versus battery-only alarms
differentiators.detail: The gap is real and measurable: 93% operation versus 79%. Almost all of the difference is human — missing or dead batteries accounted for 71% of all alarm failures and 87% of battery-only failures.

differentiators.label: Versus sealed ten-year units
differentiators.detail: Hardwired wins on reliability and interconnection; sealed units win overwhelmingly on retrofit cost. For an existing finished house, sealed is usually the right answer.

differentiators.label: The ten-year rule
differentiators.detail: Alarms are replaced ten years from the date of manufacture printed on the back — not from when you installed them, and not when the battery dies. This applies to hardwired units too, and is the most commonly ignored rule in home fire safety.

buying.where: Any hardware or big-box store, electrical wholesalers, Amazon in both countries.
buying.note: Buy all the units at once and from the same product line. Cross-brand interconnection is not reliable, and mixing generations within a brand can fail too.

install.time: 20-40 minutes per location where wiring exists; a day or more for a full retrofit
install.note: If the wiring is there, this is a swap most competent DIYers can do with the breaker off. If it is not, get an electrician — and price sealed battery units first, because they may do the job for a tenth of the cost.

ongoing.note: Test monthly with the button. Vacuum the grilles twice a year — dust is the main cause of nuisance alarms. Replace backup batteries annually, and the whole unit at ten years.

alternatives.name: Sealed ten-year lithium alarms
alternatives.note: The best retrofit. Removes the dominant failure mode without an electrician.

alternatives.name: Wireless-interconnected battery alarms
alternatives.note: Interconnection without wiring. Accepted in US retrofits; check your provincial code in Canada.

guide.verdict: If you are building, renovating, or already have the wiring, this is the configuration with the best evidence behind it. If you are not, do not open walls for it — sealed ten-year units get you most of the benefit for a fraction of the cost and disruption.

name: 10-Year Sealed Battery Smoke Alarm
priceNote: No battery to buy for a decade
summary: A battery alarm with a lithium cell sealed inside for the unit's full ten-year life. You cannot remove the battery, which is precisely the point: a missing or dead battery is the reason most failed alarms failed.
pros: Removes the single most common cause of alarm failure
No ladder trips for battery changes, and no 3 a.m. low-battery chirp
Mandatory for battery alarms sold in several US states, which tells you what regulators concluded
cons: Not interconnected unless you buy a wireless-interconnect model
Whole unit is landfill at ten years, battery included
bestFor: Any existing house without alarm wiring — which is most of them.

guide.howItWorks: Identical detection hardware to any other alarm, with a sealed lithium cell sized to last the ten-year service life of the unit. At end of life it chirps a distinct end-of-life signal and the whole thing is replaced. There is no battery door, so the alarm cannot be silenced by removing the power source — only by the hush button.
guide.market: Kidde and First Alert again dominate, with sealed versions of most of their line at CAD $25-$60. Several US states — California, Florida, Maryland, New Jersey and New York among them — now require that battery-only alarms sold there have sealed ten-year batteries, which has pushed the category from premium option to default. In Canada there is no provincial equivalent, but Montreal's agglomeration and Laval require non-removable ten-year lithium batteries in pre-1985 buildings that lack mains-powered alarms, which catches a great many Quebec homes.

features.label: Sealed lithium cell
features.detail: Not removable and not replaceable. This is a design constraint doing safety work, not a limitation.

features.label: End-of-life signal
features.detail: A distinct chirp pattern at ten years telling you to replace the unit, which is far more useful than hoping you remember the install date.

features.label: Hush button
features.detail: Silences a nuisance alarm temporarily. The existence of a hush button is what makes a sealed battery tolerable next to a kitchen.

features.label: Optional wireless interconnect
features.detail: Some sealed models link by radio so one alarm sounds them all. Costs more and is worth it in a house where a basement fire would otherwise go unheard upstairs.

costs.upfront: CAD $25-$60 per unit; CAD $45-$90 for wireless-interconnect versions.
costs.consumables: None. That is the product.
costs.ancillary: Nothing.
costs.fiveYear: Nil — you are halfway through the unit's life.

differentiators.label: Versus a 9 V alarm
differentiators.detail: Same detection, radically better real-world reliability, and no annual chore. Given that 56% of battery-only alarm failures were missing or disconnected batteries, this design change addresses most of the problem.

differentiators.label: Versus hardwired
differentiators.detail: Less reliable on paper and not interconnected by default, but installable by anyone in ten minutes at no labour cost. For a finished house the practical comparison usually favours sealed.

differentiators.label: The disposal caveat
differentiators.detail: A sealed unit is thrown away whole, lithium and all. Check whether your municipality takes them at a battery or electronics depot rather than in household waste.

buying.where: Hardware and big-box stores, pharmacies, Amazon in both countries.
buying.note: Check the date of manufacture on the back before you buy. Alarms sit in warehouses, and a unit made two years ago has eight years left, not ten.

install.time: 10 minutes per alarm
install.note: Ceiling-mounted, at least 6 ft from a photoelectric unit's nearest cooking appliance and 20 ft for ionisation. Not within 3 ft of a bathroom door. Write the install date on the unit with a marker — the manufacture date is what counts, but the install date tells you how long it has been up there.

ongoing.note: Press the test button monthly. Vacuum twice a year. Replace the unit when it signals end of life or at ten years from manufacture, whichever comes first.

alternatives.name: Hardwired interconnected alarms
alternatives.note: Better if the wiring exists. Not worth opening walls for.

alternatives.name: Replaceable-battery alarms
alternatives.note: Cheaper by a few dollars and measurably worse. No longer legal to sell as battery-only units in several US states.

guide.verdict: For an existing house this is the highest-value fire safety purchase available, and it costs about the same as lunch. Buy one for every storey and every bedroom, check the manufacture date, and put a note in your calendar for nine years from now.

name: Combination Smoke & Carbon Monoxide Alarm
pick: Two hazards, one mounting point — with a catch
priceNote: CO sensor life is the binding constraint
summary: One unit detecting both smoke and carbon monoxide. Convenient and code-acceptable in most places, with a genuine drawback that almost nobody is told about: the CO sensor wears out years before the smoke sensor does.
pros: One device, one mounting point, one thing to test
Required coverage for both hazards where a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage exists
Often cheaper than buying two separate alarms
cons: CO sensors typically last about seven years against the smoke alarm's ten — the shorter life governs
Ideal mounting height for smoke and for CO are not the same, so one function is compromised
bestFor: Homes with a fuel-burning appliance, fireplace or attached garage, where CO coverage is required anyway.

guide.howItWorks: Two sensors in one housing: a photoelectric or ionisation smoke sensor, and an electrochemical cell that reacts to carbon monoxide. They alarm with different sound patterns — the three-pulse temporal pattern for fire, four pulses for CO — because the correct response differs. Fire means get out. CO means get to fresh air and call for help, and the distinction matters.
guide.market: Every major alarm brand sells combination units, CAD $35-$90, in sealed, replaceable-battery and hardwired versions. The standards are UL 217 for the smoke side and UL 2034 in the US, CAN/CSA-6.19 in Canada, for the CO side. The category has grown quickly because Canadian provinces have progressively mandated CO alarms — Ontario expanded its requirement to every storey as of January 2026 — and a combination unit is the path of least resistance to compliance.

features.label: Distinct alarm patterns
features.detail: Three pulses for fire, four for CO. Better units announce which hazard in speech, which removes a genuinely dangerous ambiguity at 3 a.m.

features.label: CO detection thresholds
features.detail: UL 2034 requires an alarm within 60-240 minutes at 70 ppm, 10-50 minutes at 150 ppm, and 4-15 minutes at 400 ppm — and requires the unit not to alarm below 30 ppm. Advocacy groups argue that floor is too high for infants, pregnant people and cardiac patients; low-level monitors exist outside the standard.

features.label: End-of-life signal
features.detail: More important here than on a smoke-only alarm, because the CO cell expires first and a silently dead CO sensor is invisible.

features.label: Sealed or replaceable
features.detail: Sealed ten-year combination units exist, but check whether the manufacturer rates the CO function for the full ten years — many do not.

costs.upfront: CAD $35-$90 per unit.
costs.consumables: Batteries on replaceable models.
costs.ancillary: Nothing.
costs.fiveYear: You will likely be replacing the unit around year seven rather than year ten, so budget for one full replacement cycle sooner than a smoke-only alarm.

differentiators.label: Versus separate alarms
